helpText: CMH tests the association between a row variable and a column variable while controlling for (stratifying on) a third variable. The row, column, and stratum variables must all be categorical (factors). The common odds ratio and the homogeneity tests (Breslow-Day, Woolf) are only defined for the 2 x 2 x K case (row and column each have exactly two levels).
title: Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) Test
weight: Frequency / count variable (optional, if data is already tabulated)
correct: Apply continuity correction (2 x 2 x K only)
conflevel: Confidence level for the common odds ratio
label2: Homogeneity of odds ratios (2 x 2 x K only)
label3: Generalized CMH (for ordered categories, via coin)
gencmh: Generalized CMH tests (general association + linear-by-linear trend)
showindiv: Show an unstratified chi-square test for each stratum

help.title: Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) Test
help.body:
What is the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test?
The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test measures whether two categorical variables are associated after accounting for a third categorical variable that divides the data into strata. In plain terms, it answers "are these two things related once I hold the confounder constant?" It works by forming a separate contingency table within each stratum, measuring the association in each one, and then combining those stratum-specific associations into a single pooled test. Because the pooling happens within strata, an imbalance in the stratifying variable across groups cannot by itself create a spurious association or mask a real one.

A clinical trial example
Suppose a trial compares an active drug against placebo, and the outcome is whether each patient responded (yes/no). Patients were enrolled at several hospitals, and the hospitals differ in baseline response rate and in how many patients they contributed to each arm. Comparing response between arms with a single pooled 2x2 table would let those site differences leak into the treatment comparison. A CMH test stratified by site compares treatment and response within each hospital and then combines the evidence, giving a site-adjusted test of the treatment effect plus a common odds ratio that summarises the drug's benefit across sites. This "control for a stratification factor" pattern (site, baseline severity, region) is one of the most common uses of CMH in confirmatory trials.

Description
Performs the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test of conditional independence between a row variable and a column variable, controlling for one or more stratifying variables. Internally builds a contingency table with xtabs() and calls mantelhaen.test() from the stats package. Optionally reports the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio with a confidence interval, tests the assumption that the odds ratio is constant across strata (Breslow-Day and Woolf tests), and computes generalized CMH statistics for ordered categories.

The CMH test asks whether the row and column variables are associated once the stratifying variable is held constant. It is the categorical-data counterpart to adjusting for a confounder, and is widely used in clinical trials to compare a binary outcome across treatment arms while controlling for a stratification factor such as site or baseline severity.

NOTE
1. The row, column, and stratum variables must all be categorical (factors). Convert numeric variables with Data > Factor Levels if needed.
2. The common odds ratio, its confidence interval, and the Breslow-Day and Woolf homogeneity tests are only defined when the row and column variables each have exactly two levels (a 2 x 2 x K design). For larger tables the dialog reports the general association chi-square from mantelhaen.test() and, if requested, the generalized CMH tests, but not a common odds ratio.
3. The homogeneity tests answer a different question from the CMH test itself. A significant Breslow-Day or Woolf result means the odds ratio differs across strata (effect modification), in which case a single common odds ratio is not a good summary and stratum-specific estimates should be reported instead. The regulatory convention is to run the homogeneity test first and only report the common odds ratio if it is not significant.
4. If your data is already tabulated (one row per cell with a count column), specify that count column as the frequency variable. Otherwise leave it blank and each row of the dataset is treated as one observation.

Usage
#Build the stratified table (row x column x stratum)
BSkyTable <- xtabs(~ outcome + treatment + site, data = Dataset1)
#Core CMH test
mantelhaen.test(BSkyTable, correct = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
#Homogeneity of the odds ratio across strata (2 x 2 x K only)
DescTools::BreslowDayTest(BSkyTable)
vcd::woolf_test(BSkyTable)
#Generalized CMH for ordered categories (uses the coin package)
coin::cmh_test(outcome ~ treatment | site, data = Dataset1)  #general association
coin::lbl_test(outcome ~ treatment | site, data = Dataset1)  #linear-by-linear (ordinal trend)
Arguments
  • Row variable: the first categorical variable, often the outcome (e.g. response yes/no).
  • Column variable: the second categorical variable, often the exposure or treatment group.
  • Stratum variable(s): the categorical variable(s) to control for. With more than one, their combinations define the strata.
  • Frequency variable: an optional count column when the data is already summarised to one row per table cell.
Trying it out with the sample datasets
Two datasets are provided to exercise the dialog. Before running either, use Data > Factor Levels to confirm the variables are factors (and, for the ordinal example, that the levels are in a meaningful order).

1. cmh_test_data (a 2 x 2 x K design: binary outcome, binary treatment, several sites)
This dataset has a binary RESPONSE (Yes/No), a binary TREATMENT (Active/Placebo), and a 4-level SITE. It demonstrates the classic stratified 2x2 analysis with a common odds ratio.
  • Row variable: RESPONSE
  • Column variable: TREATMENT
  • Stratum / control variable(s): SITE
  • Frequency / count variable: leave blank (one row per subject).
Options to select: check Apply continuity correction, leave the confidence level at 0.95, and check Breslow-Day test (optionally Woolf test as a second homogeneity check). Leave Generalized CMH unchecked, because both variables are nominal, not ordered. Show the stratified contingency table is helpful for seeing the counts. Because this is a 2 x 2 x K table you will get the CMH test, a common odds ratio reported in both directions (with an orientation note naming the exact levels used), and a non-significant Breslow-Day result indicating the odds ratio is consistent across sites.
A pre-tabulated version, cmh_test_data_freq, contains the same data summarised to one row per cell with a Freq count column; to use it, select the same row/column/stratum variables and put Freq in the frequency variable field.

2. cmh_ordinal_data (a larger 4 x 4 x 2 design with an ordinal dose-response)
This dataset has an ordinal RESPONSE (None < Mild < Moderate < Marked), an ordinal DOSE (Placebo < Low < Medium < High), and a 2-level SEX. It demonstrates the generalized CMH tests and the behaviour of the dialog when the table is larger than 2 x 2 x K.
  • Row variable: RESPONSE
  • Column variable: DOSE
  • Stratum / control variable(s): SEX
  • Frequency / count variable: leave blank.
Important: first reorder the levels of RESPONSE and DOSE (Data > Factor Levels) so they run from lowest to highest, because the linear-by-linear test scores the levels in the order they appear. Options to select: check Generalized CMH tests. You may leave Breslow-Day and Woolf checked to confirm they correctly decline (they require a 2 x 2 x K table), and continuity correction has no effect here. Because this is not a 2 x 2 x K table you will see: the general-association CMH chi-square, a message explaining that no common odds ratio is reported, the generalized CMH general-association test, and a linear-by-linear (correlation) test that should be strongly significant because response increases monotonically with dose. The general-association table also carries a footnote about regulatory reporting conventions for tables larger than 2 x 2 x K.
